S031.name: Diminished_Thinking
S031.description: Diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness.

subtypes.Reduced Concentration: Unable to pay attention or maintain focus on specific activities like conversation, reading, or watching TV.
subtypes.Indecisiveness: Extreme difficulty making even minor daily choices (e.g., menu, clothes) and hesitating to make decisions.
subtypes.Subjective Memory Complaints: Complaining of memory decline, such as forgetting where things were placed, due to reduced focus.
subtypes.Clouded Thinking: Thinking feels foggy, dazed, or not clear.

S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.

subtypes.Intrusive Memories: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Distressing Dreams: Recurrent distressing dreams in which the content and/or affect of the dream are related to the traumatic event.
subtypes.Dissociative Reactions (Flashbacks): Dissociative reactions (e.g., flashbacks) in which the individual feels or acts as if the traumatic event were recurring.
subtypes.Psychological Distress at Cues: Intense or prolonged psychological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Physiological Reactions to Cues: Marked physiological reactions to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.

S070.name: Trauma_Avoidance
S070.description: Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event.

subtypes.Internal Avoidance: Efforts to avoid distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings about or closely associated with the traumatic event.
subtypes.External Avoidance: Efforts to avoid external reminders (people, places, conversations, activities, objects, situations) that arouse distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.

subtypes.Impulsive Anger: Sudden explosions of anger for trivial reasons or no clear reason.
subtypes.Verbal Aggression: Attacking others with shouting, cursing, or blame without holding back.
subtypes.Physical Aggression: Physically attacking people or throwing/breaking objects.
subtypes.Chronic Irritability: A state where nerves are always sharp and sensitive, ready to explode at the slightest touch.

S080.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
S080.description: Exaggerated startle response to minor stimuli.

subtypes.Auditory Startle: Startling excessively and flinching physically at sudden noises.
subtypes.Tactile Startle: Being extremely startled by unexpected physical contact.
subtypes.Visual Startle: Being greatly startled and wary of sudden appearances of people or rapid movements.
subtypes.Slow Recovery: Heart pounding and trembling for a long time after being startled, not calming down easily.

S082.name: Depersonalization_Derealization
S082.description: Altered sense of the reality of one's self or surroundings after a traumatic event.

subtypes.Depersonalization: Feeling detached from one's own body or mental processes, as if being an outside observer.
subtypes.Derealization: The surrounding environment feels unreal, dreamlike, distant, or distorted.
subtypes.Time Distortion: Time feels like it has stopped during the traumatic moment, or is perceived as moving extremely slowly or quickly.

symptom.disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is a trauma- and stressor-related condition that emerges within days of exposure to a severe traumatic event involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation, either directly experienced, witnessed, or learned about occurring to a close other. It is characterized by a cluster of intrusive memories, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and marked arousal, lasting from at least 3 days up to 1 month after the trauma, and causing significant distress or functional impairment. Clinically, ASD often presents with sudden changes in functioning at work or home, emotional numbing or agitation, and difficulty integrating the traumatic experience into ongoing life. It is distinguished from Posttraumatic Stress Disorder primarily by its shorter duration and more prominent dissociative symptoms early on, though it confers increased risk for later PTSD if symptoms persist or worsen.

patient.stressor: Two weeks before presentation, Angelina was driving home after a late closing shift at the store when another car ran a red light and T-boned her vehicle at a downtown Honolulu intersection. Although she escaped with only minor physical injuries and the other driver survived, she was trapped in the car for several minutes, surrounded by shattered glass and the smell of burning rubber, while bystanders and first responders worked to get her out. In the days that followed, her usually structured routines around hiking, yoga, and creative work began to unravel, and she found herself increasingly unable to complete merchandising plans or concentrate on digital design tasks she previously enjoyed. After nearly missing an important store reset because she could not bring herself to drive to work and her manager gently confronted her about her sudden drop in performance and focus, her older cousin—who had also noticed her withdrawing from family and cultural activities—encouraged her to see a mental health professional through the clinic affiliated with her employer.
patient.chief_complaint: “Ever since the car accident I just can’t think straight or focus long enough to finish anything, even simple tasks at work.”

S031.name: Diminished_Thinking
S031.description: Diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness.
S031.manifestation: At work now I’ll open an email or a planogram and just stare at it, reading the same line over and over until my mind goes totally blank and I can’t even decide something simple like which display to start on, so I end up doing nothing and falling behind.

S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
S069.manifestation: All day and especially when I’m trying to relax, these pictures of the crash just pop into my head—the sound of the other car slamming into me, the glass everywhere, the smell of burning rubber—and my heart starts racing like I’m back in the driver’s seat again and I can’t shut it off.

S070.name: Trauma_Avoidance
S070.description: Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event.
S070.manifestation: I’ve been going way out of my way to avoid that whole intersection and I make excuses when friends or family want to drive anywhere at night, because even thinking about being in a car after dark makes my chest tighten and I feel like I might lose it.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.
S077.manifestation: Lately the smallest things set me off—like my sister asking a basic question about the car insurance—and I’ll snap at her or my coworkers, raising my voice and getting all sharp before I even realize how angry I sound.

S080.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
S080.description: Exaggerated startle response to minor stimuli.
S080.manifestation: Ever since the accident, if someone drops a hanger in the stockroom or a car honks outside the store I literally jump out of my skin, my whole body jerks, my heart is pounding, and it takes a long time for me to calm down again.

S082.name: Depersonalization_Derealization
S082.description: Altered sense of the reality of one's self or surroundings after a traumatic event.
S082.manifestation: Sometimes when I’m riding in a car or even just walking down the street, everything suddenly feels weirdly far away and fake, like I’m watching a movie of my own life and not really in my body, and I kind of space out until it slowly wears off.
